messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Eighth protocol. Its genome changes in waves. Visible mutations are only the easiest part to understand.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Other changes remain internal: reflexes, fear, attachment, capacity to learn. Faced with these mutations, what priority do you choose?

choices.label: I stabilize its current form before it loses coherence.
I model the mutations before choosing what to correct.
I do not correct anomalies as long as they still give it options.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: We can correct an anomaly, but the correction may also remove a possibility. What do you correct, and what do you leave alive?

choices.label: I correct what could make it dangerous to others.
I correct only what makes it suffer.
I keep a record and let it adapt a little longer.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Chen insists: the remaining anomalies are defects to correct if we want to approach perfection. Still, choose what the protocol will not strip away yet.

choices.label: It will be too protective, but it will hold against danger.
It will be too curious, but it can learn beyond us.
It will be too bonded, but it will not grow up abandoned.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You are trying to freeze something alive. Useful for us, perhaps violent for it.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: It is the slowest answer, and often the least spectacular. It is still the most honest.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You prioritize collective safety. It is defensible, but every correction leaves a mark on what it might have become.
